# Translate a Foreign Email or PDF on Your PC With ChatRTX

> **In short:** ChatRTX is a free desktop app from NVIDIA that translates and summarizes documents fully on your own computer, with no internet needed. Paste a foreign-language email or drop in a PDF, ask in plain English, and you'll get a translation plus a one-paragraph summary of what the sender is actually asking for.

Have you ever stared at a long email from a supplier overseas or a PDF attachment from a relative abroad, trying to guess what they really want? ChatRTX is built for exactly this moment. It runs an AI model locally on your Windows PC (an **LLM** — a large language model, the same kind of "brain" that powers ChatGPT), so you can paste text or load a file and ask questions in plain English. Nothing leaves your machine, which is helpful if the email contains private details you'd rather not upload anywhere.

## Before you start

- **A Windows PC with a recent NVIDIA graphics card.** ChatRTX needs a GeForce RTX 30-series, 40-series or 50-series GPU (the graphics-processing chip inside your computer). You can check by pressing **Win + R**, typing `dxdiag`, and hitting Enter — the "Display" tab will list your card model.
- **About 15 GB of free disk space.** The app and its default AI model together take roughly that much. SSDs work best; old spinning hard drives will feel slow.
- **A recent copy of Windows 10 or Windows 11.** Anything from the last few years is fine.
- **Roughly 20–30 minutes the first time.** Installing the app and the default model is the slow part; the actual translating takes seconds.
- **No account, no subscription.** ChatRTX is free to download from NVIDIA. You will need to create a free NVIDIA developer account to download it, but you do not pay anything.
- **A short document to try.** Have one foreign-language email (you can paste it as text) or one PDF ready so your first run actually does something useful.

## Step 1 — Download and install ChatRTX

Open your web browser and go to the official NVIDIA product page for **ChatRTX**. Look for a button labeled something like **Download** or **Get Started**. Click it, then sign in with your NVIDIA developer account (or create one — it only asks for an email and a password). After the installer file finishes downloading, double-click it and follow the on-screen prompts. The installer may ask you to confirm a folder and agree to the license terms.

💬 Example: when the installer asks where to put the app, the default location (`C:\Program Files\NVIDIA\ChatRTX`) is fine — leave it as is unless you have a strong reason to change it.

You'll know it worked when a new icon named **ChatRTX** appears in your Start menu and you can launch it without an error message.

## Step 2 — Install your first AI model

The first time ChatRTX opens, the main window shows an empty chat area and a sidebar (the narrow panel on the left or right) with a section labeled something like **Models** or **AI Models**. That section is empty — the app itself is just a window; the actual "brain" (the LLM) is a separate download. Click the button that says **Download** next to the model named **Mistral** or **Llama** (NVIDIA changes the default model name from time to time, so look for whichever one has a "Download" button beside it). A progress bar appears; let it finish — this is the biggest download, so it may take several minutes on a slow connection. If your hard drive seems too small, try the smaller "Mistral 7B" option first.

💬 Example: if the sidebar shows two models and you can only fit one, choose the one with the smaller number — for example "Mistral 7B" rather than a 13B model. Smaller models translate a touch less smoothly but run on more PCs.

You'll know it worked when the model name in the sidebar no longer has a "Download" button next to it and instead shows a small green dot or a check mark.

## Step 3 — Paste the foreign-language email into the chat

Click inside the chat box at the bottom of the window (it usually has placeholder text like "Type a message…" or "Ask me anything…"). Then go to the foreign-language email in your browser or mail app, select the whole message with **Ctrl + A**, copy it with **Ctrl + C**, and paste it into the chat box with **Ctrl + V**. The text appears in your language. Press **Enter** to send. A short pause later — usually a few seconds — the model's answer streams in line by line.

💬 Example: if you paste a three-paragraph email in German and just hit Enter, the model will likely respond in English. To steer it, use the prompt in the next step instead.

You'll know it worked when text starts appearing word by word in the chat area, and the model ends with a clear English paragraph rather than an error message.

## Step 4 — Ask for the translation and the summary in one go

Now send a follow-up message that tells the model exactly what you need. A good instruction names the source language, the target language, and the extra thing you want (a summary of the ask). Think of the chat box as a place where you write the **prompt** — the instruction you give the AI. The more specific the prompt, the better the answer.

💬 Example: `Please translate the email above from German to English, then give me a 3-sentence summary of what the sender is actually asking me to do and by when.`

If you don't know the source language, ask the model to detect it first:

💬 Example: `First tell me what language the text above is written in. Then translate it to English and summarize what the sender wants.`

You'll know it worked when the reply has two clearly separated parts: a translation and a short summary that names an action, a date, or a question the sender is asking about.

## Step 5 — Add a PDF instead of plain text

For longer documents, you don't have to copy and paste by hand. Look near the chat box for a small **paperclip icon**, an **attachment icon**, or a button labeled **Add file** or **Upload document**. Click it, browse to the PDF on your computer, and select it. The file name appears above the chat box. Now type a prompt that refers to "the attached document" rather than "the text above."

💬 Example: `Read the attached PDF (it is in Spanish). Translate the whole thing to English and then list, in bullet form, every request or deadline the document mentions.`

If you don't see a paperclip icon, look inside a **+** (plus) button, a **⋯** (three dots) menu, or a separate **Documents** tab in the sidebar — NVIDIA occasionally moves this control between releases. You can also fall back to opening the PDF in another program, selecting all with **Ctrl + A**, and pasting the text into the chat as in Step 3; PDFs that are scanned images won't paste as text, in which case you'll need an OCR step (a tool that reads text out of images) first.

You'll know it worked when the model writes back using details from the PDF — names, dates, amounts — that you never typed into the chat yourself.

## Step 6 — Save the translation for later

Most people want to keep the translation somewhere they can find it again. Click anywhere inside the model's reply in the chat to place your cursor there, then press **Ctrl + A** to select the whole answer and **Ctrl + C** to copy it. Open any text editor — Notepad, Word, Google Docs — and paste with **Ctrl + V**. Give the file a clear name like `Supplier-email-translation-2026.txt`. ChatRTX itself does not have a built-in "save" button, so this copy-and-paste step is how you keep a record.

💬 Example: name the file after the sender and the date, for example `Acme-supplier-2026-06-04.txt`, so you can search for it later in your Documents folder.

You'll know it worked when you can close ChatRTX, reopen the saved file, and read the translation without launching the app again.

## Common mistakes

- **Installing the app but forgetting to download a model.** The chat box looks ready, but every reply will be an error. The fix: go back to the **Models** section in the sidebar and click **Download** next to the default model. Wait for it to finish before trying again.
- **Pasting a scanned PDF (an image of text) instead of a real text PDF.** Scanned PDFs look like documents but contain pictures, not selectable words. The fix: run the PDF through an OCR tool first (many free ones exist online), or paste a real text version of the email if you have one.
- **Asking for "a translation" without saying the source or target language.** The model may guess, and guesses can be wrong for short messages. The fix: always name both languages in your prompt, for example "translate from Japanese to English." If you don't know the source language, ask the model to detect it first (Step 4 has a ready-made prompt for this).

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** That forwarded email from a relative traveling abroad, the school newsletter in your neighbor's language, the rental contract attachment from a future landlord — any of these can be translated and summarized in under a minute, on your own computer, with no data sent to a cloud server.
- **For your business or work:** A supplier invoice, a customs document, a partner's terms-of-service PDF — ChatRTX turns a stressful pile of unfamiliar text into a short list of what you actually need to do and by when. Because everything stays local, it's a reasonable choice for documents that contain customer names, prices or other details you'd rather not paste into a public website.
- **If you're just getting started:** The single easiest first move is to paste one short email you've been ignoring and ask for a translation plus a one-sentence summary of the ask. Treat the reply as a draft, not a final word — for anything official (a contract, a legal letter), have a human translator confirm the meaning before you act on it.

## Try it now

Open ChatRTX, paste the first paragraph of any foreign-language email you've been putting off, and send this single prompt:

💬 `Translate this to English, then tell me in one sentence what the sender wants me to do.`

In under a minute you'll have a plain-English version and the actual question hidden in the message. That's the whole point of having a translator on your own PC — the hard part is no longer the language; it's just deciding what to reply.
